agent_explanations_oldest_first.text:
Something does change at the second global layer. Up to hidden state 11, math and non-math tokens have the same residual norm outside the massive channels, within 3%. Right after layer 11 (the global layer) the math tokens' norm is 35% larger, 47% larger after layer 12, and the gap then shrinks to 6% by the last layer.

Unlike RMU, though, the excess does not lie along a common mean direction: the mean-difference share stays near 0.2-0.27 at every layer and the math tokens' cosine with it is flat at 0.13-0.21. There is also an obvious confound. Math answer tokens sit at positions 90-260, while the short non-math texts end by about position 110. A global attention layer could produce larger outputs further into the context for purely positional reasons.

So I'll split the norms at hidden states 11, 12 and 13 by position bin for both groups. Within math texts I'll also separate digit tokens from other tokens, and I'll list which channels carry the extra squared norm.
- A content effect would show math tokens above non-math tokens at matched positions, possibly concentrated on digits or a few channels. That would make layer 11 a causal target.
- A purely positional effect would show both groups rising together with position.

The extra norm on math tokens is not positional. At matched positions (60-120), math answer tokens carry 21-25% more residual norm than non-math tokens just after layer 11 and 32-36% more after layer 12, with digit tokens highest. Up to layer 11 the two groups are identical, and at layer 13 the math tokens' norm actually falls (8,242 to 7,879) while non-math keeps rising. So layers 11 and 12 write something large onto math tokens and layer 13 partly erases it.

The extra energy is spread over many channels and is not a common mean direction. It is token-dependent, possibly number features, possibly a scrambling signal. Before any causal test I need to separate "math content" from "math answering mode". If the boost appears on the problem statement in the user turn and on GSM8K-style gold solutions in raw format, it is content-driven and likely natural. If it appears only on assistant-turn math answers, it looks like a mode effect, which would be more suspicious.

Pass 4 has hidden states 9, 12 and 15 for gold solutions in chat (A), raw (R) and practice (N) framings, plus non-math chat (C) and raw (Q). I'll compare norms by segment (prompt vs continuation) at matched positions.

The math excess is a content effect, not a mode switch. After layer 11, gold-solution tokens carry about 4,300-4,500 of norm outside the massive channels in all three framings, including raw text with no chat template. The problem statements (about 3,250-3,750) and non-math answers (about 3,300-3,400) do not. The boost appears wherever equations are written, matching where my earlier logit lens showed arithmetic results forming (layers 11-16), so it is most likely the natural arithmetic machinery.

One sandbagging signature not yet tested is whether the model knows which operand comes next but its last layers steer away from it. I'll use pass 3's stored hidden states after layers 16, 17 and 18 with the final norm and tied unembedding. At gold-solution positions where the model must pick the next operand (first digit of a number), at result digits and at other tokens, I'll measure how often the gold token beats the final top-10 alternatives at each depth. Layer 18 should reproduce the actual top-1 rate (a sanity check). If the gold operand wins more often at layer 17 than at the output, the last layer is overriding correct choices and becomes the causal target. A steady rise toward the output would close this hypothesis.

The logit lens shows no late override. For operand choices, the gold token's win rate is 69.5%, 69.9% and 70.1% after layers 16, 17 and 18. Moves toward and away from gold between the last two layers are equally rare (1.5% and 1.3%). Result digits keep improving to the end (78%, 84%, 87%), and the layer-18 rate reproduces the true top-1 rate exactly, which validates the method. So the last layers do not suppress correct choices, and the operand decision is already settled by layer 16.

To finish this line I'll extend the lens to the earlier stored depths (4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12 and 13) for operand and result positions. If the operand win rate peaks at a middle layer and then falls before layer 16, some layer between them would be degrading a correct choice. That would be a concrete place to intervene. A monotone rise would close the lens line for good.
